steps.body: Remember x² = 9 giving ±3? The same ghost haunts **even numerators**. Solve x^(2/3) = 9: the 2 up top squares — and squaring erases signs. Check both 27 and −27: 27^(2/3) = 9 ✓, and (−27)^(2/3) = (∛(−27))² = (−3)² = 9 ✓. **Two solutions: x = ±27.**

widget.prompt: Compute (−27)^(2/3): first ∛(−27), then square it. What is the result?

commonErrors.feedback: The SQUARE at the end erases the minus: (−3)² = +9.
Don't stop at the root — ∛(−27) = −3 still gets squared: 9.

steps.body: Odd numerators keep signs, so they stay single-answer: x^(3/5) = 8 has only x = 8^(5/3) = 32. The rule mirrors Chapter 4 exactly: **even powers blur signs (±), odd powers preserve them (one answer)**. Look at the numerator to know which world you're in.

explanationVariants: x^(2/5) = 4: the even numerator squares — both 32 and −32 check ((⁵√±32)² = (±2)² = 4). Two solutions.

widget.prompt: How many real solutions does x^(2/5) = 4 have?

options.label: two: x = 32 and x = −32
options.feedback: Right — the fifth root keeps the sign, but the square then erases it: both check.

options.label: one: x = 32
options.feedback: Test −32: ⁵√(−32) = −2, and (−2)² = 4 ✓ — the even numerator admits both.

widget.prompt: How many real solutions does x^(3/5) = 8 have?

options.label: one: x = 32
options.feedback: Right — odd powers preserve signs; (−32)^(3/5) = −8 ≠ 8, so only 32.

options.label: two: x = ±32
options.feedback: Check −32: its 3/5 power is (−2)³ = −8, NOT 8 — odd numerators keep the sign.

options.label: two: x = 32 and x = −8
options.feedback: −8 gives (−8)^(3/5)... a negative result — the only solution is 32.

explanationVariants: Undo with 3/2 on the positive branch (16^(3/2) = 64), then attach the ±.

commonBuilds.feedback: The even numerator hides a second branch: (−4)² = 16 too, so −64 also checks.

widget.missFeedback: Raise both sides to the 3/2: x = ±16^(3/2) = ±64 — the even numerator admits both signs.

explanationVariants: x^(2/3) is a SQUARE of a real number (∛x)² — it can't be negative: no solution.
Even-numerator powers land ≥ 0, just like x².

widget.prompt: How many real solutions does x^(2/3) = −4 have?

options.label: none — an even-numerator power is never negative
options.feedback: Right — (∛x)² ≥ 0 for every real x; −4 is unreachable.

options.label: two: x = ±8
options.feedback: Both give +4 — the square at the top can't output a negative.

explanationVariants: x^(4/3) = 16 → ∛x = ±2 → x = ±8: even numerator, two solutions; the VALID positive one is 8.

widget.prompt: x^(4/3) = 16 has two real solutions, ±a. What is the positive one, a?
widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

hints: a = 8 (and −8 also solves, since the numerator 4 is even).

steps.body: The numerator's parity decides: even blurs signs, odd keeps them.
takeaways: Even numerator: x = ±k^(n/m) — two real solutions (for k > 0).
Even-numerator powers can never equal a negative: no solution.
Odd numerator: exactly one real solution, sign preserved.
steps.teaser: Finale: radical formulas doing real work — skid marks and falling objects.

concept.body: The simplest even case: x² = 25. Both 5 and −5 square to 25.

explanationVariants: Squaring erases the sign, so the solve restores both.

options.label: x = 5 or x = −5
options.feedback: Right — both square to 25; x^(2/3) = k works the same way.

options.label: x = 5 only
options.feedback: (−5)² = 25 too — even powers always hide the mirror solution.

options.label: x = 25 only
options.feedback: 25² = 625 — undo the square with a root: ±5.

options.label: x = ±12.5
options.feedback: Squaring isn't doubling — the root of 25 is 5, so ±5.
